rv.q: This new 'Camelot' doesn't quite achieve the impossible dream of its legendary predecessor, but it succeeds in making Lerner and Loewe's score feel vital again.
The result is an at times dramatically lagging, but consistently polished and warming tale playing out at Lincoln Center’s Theater.
And as this lavish but less than lustrous production unfolds, that aforementioned sense of impending bad weather never seems to let up.
The revival makes you want to believe in a great musical called Camelot, even if such a thing never did exist.

It moves like a funeral procession for itself.
Neither, it seems, is sufficient today.
It’s the chilliest “Camelot” you ever did see and it embodies so many of the current neuroses surrounding the revival of classic American musicals.
Indeed, this Camelot, which I admittedly could not muster up much enthusiasm for upon entering the Theater, was surprisingly engaging.

Reinvigorated by Sorkin — who has long painted a dreamy, egalitarian view of politics within his works — and his new book, the musical succeeds in evoking that dream for one brief, shining moment once again.

If this Camelot is a bit confused on whether it wants to be a majestic golden age musical or a gritty take on the shaky foundations of a monarchical ménage à trois, it pulls through on the strength of its cast, which tightly brings the work’s brief shining moment into glorious light.
It’s a shame that this “Camelot,” despite its shining moments and impeccable pedigree, doesn’t offer more of that kind of splendor.
As beautifully sung as this new Camelot is – and it is – the production nearly scuttles romance along with the magic.
But, as entertaining as the musical numbers are, it’s hard not to be disappointed by this production.
Sher's direction is also a marvel when Sorkin's book is at its messiest.
Ultimately, though, this Camelot revival falls on its own sword with its reworked book.

Due to Sorkin’s undernourished scribing, the emotions the songs reveal don’t fit the emotion-deprived characters.
At almost three hours on a spartan stage, it grinds into a numbingly boring show.
Camelot was maybe not the most obvious of theatre productions to reconfigure, yet Sorkin’s book and stunning lead performances make this truly next level.
Indeed, the choice to hide such crucial information up Sorkin's sleeve is not just misguided magic, but the most bizarre thing about this new, often-pleasing adaptation.
And magic is exactly what this Camelot most obviously lacks.
So smoothed out has the story become that the actors – admirable all – can do little more than stay afloat.
The result is Sorkin’s retrofitted play, where mostly incongruous songs with erudite lyrics infrequently pop in.
It is to be hoped that future musical revivals of golden age shows will either trust the original material or their audiences to know that things were different in earlier decades.
The result is arid, a musical that can't decide why anyone is singing.
